instantiated_cells.justification: “Lobbying” is defined as attempting to influence legislative or administrative action by oral or written communication and includes appearances at public hearings or meetings, covering oral, written, and event-like appearances.

The statute defines a “lobbyist” functionally as an individual paid/retained by a principal whose duties include lobbying (with a 5-days-per-reporting-period trigger if duties are mixed) and does not enumerate specific lobbyist actor types such as law firms or consultancies.
The definitions section provides terms such as “agency,” “principal,” and “business entity” but does not define “public entity” as a term.

Coverage depends on monetary and activity thresholds, including principal registration only after exceeding $500 in a calendar year, a verified-statement exemption up to $500, and lobbyist status for mixed-duty individuals only if they lobby on at least 5 days per reporting period.
“Lobbying” includes attempts to influence “legislative action,” which expressly includes the governor’s approving or vetoing bills and development of proposals for introduction in the legislature.
Lobbying is communication with “elective state official,” “agency official,” or “legislative employee,” capturing legislative-branch personnel and executive/administrative officials.
The definition of lobbying reaches attempts to influence “legislative action,” which includes the governor’s approval/veto actions, thus covering executive officials including the governor.

Because “administrative action” is agency rulemaking and “lobbying” includes attempts to influence administrative action by communicating with “agency officials,” the definition covers executive/administrative officials.
Lobbying is defined as attempts to influence legislative action by communication with “legislative employees” (including legislators) and other specified officials.

The statute defines lobbying targets as elective state officials, agency officials, and legislative employees, which encompasses legislative and executive/administrative branch officials and staff involved in official actions.

Registration/licensing obligations attach to paid lobbyists and principals, while elective state officials and legislative employees are expressly not subject to key lobbying requirements when acting in an official capacity.

The statute separately regulates agency employees paid a salary whose regular duties include influencing legislative action via agency statements, and the lobbyist definition includes paid individuals plus a time/day standard (5 days per reporting period) for mixed duties.
Covered entities and definitions turn on being a principal/employer or agency, not on public charter or special government protection as a definitional criterion.
“Principal” is defined by employing a lobbyist, and the statute does not define coverage based on ownership characteristics.
Principal registration and definitions do not rely on an entity’s structure or revenue composition beyond requiring identification of the entity’s nature/purpose and business activity.
